items.q: The film of the 1969 moon landings cannot be ___.
It wasn’t a ___ mistake — nobody meant to do it.
The show received high ___ from the critics.

acts.title: Text A · Four things people believe about the moon
text: The first is that the landings were faked. This began with the flag, which appeared to flutter in a wind that could not exist. It did not: the flag had a horizontal rod sewn into it, and it was still moving because nobody had steadied it after planting it.

The second is that a supermoon causes tsunamis. The moon does affect the tides, but it does so by a very small amount — nothing like enough. Tsunamis have occurred at the same time as supermoons, and such occurrences are coincidence.
The third is that the far side is permanently dark. That is simply wrong. It receives sunlight exactly as often as the side we see; what it never does is face us.
The fourth is that a full moon changes human behaviour. Several studies have looked for this. None has found it.

items.q: What is Text A doing?
o: Examining four common beliefs about the moon and testing them
Explaining how to see the moon
Arguing that the landings were faked

items.q: Why did the flag appear to move?
o: It had a rod sewn into it and had just been planted
There is wind on the moon

acts.title: Text B · The one that is true
text: There is a fifth belief, and this one is largely correct: without the moon, life on Earth would be much harder.

The reason is the axis. A planet’s axis can tilt, and when it does so dramatically the consequences are severe. On Mars it has tilted far enough for the polar ice to slide down towards the equator. The moon’s presence keeps ours comparatively steady.

If it disappeared, the Earth would sometimes lie almost on its side. That would produce extreme temperatures and wildly different lengths of daylight. Large parts of Africa would occasionally be covered in ice, which would make them impossible to live in.
At other times the planet would turn on a straighter axis, and if it did so there would be no seasons at all. The Earth itself would survive. We are the part that would find it difficult.

items.s: The fifth belief is described as largely correct.
The moon helps to keep the Earth’s axis steady.
On Mars the axis has tilted enough to move polar ice towards the equator.
Without the moon the Earth itself would be destroyed.
A straighter axis would produce more extreme seasons.

acts.title: What does each word point back to?
text: The first is that the landings were faked. This began with the flag.
The moon does affect the tides, but it does so by a very small amount.
The third is that the far side is permanently dark. That is simply wrong.
A planet’s axis can tilt, and when it does so the consequences are severe.
That would produce extreme temperatures and different lengths of daylight.
The Earth itself would survive. We are the part that would find it difficult.

items.q: “This began with the flag.” What does this refer to?
o: The belief that the landings were faked

items.q: “it does so by a very small amount.” What does do so replace?
“That is simply wrong.” What does that refer to?
o: The belief that the far side is permanently dark

items.q: “That would produce extreme temperatures.” What does that refer to?
o: The Earth lying almost on its side

items.q: Why do writers use these words at all?
o: To avoid repeating a whole phrase or idea
To make the text shorter for no reason

acts.title: Pointing backwards without repeating yourself
rule: Good writing rarely says the same phrase twice. Instead it points back, and the reader is expected to follow. At B2 the skill runs both ways: you have to work out what somebody else’s reference word means, and use your own without leaving the reader guessing.
points: Point back at a whole idea, not just a noun. this is usually closer or more immediate; that is more distant or more dismissive.
Usually points back at a specific thing already named. It can refer to a whole idea, but that is the safer choice when you do.
Replace a countable noun. I’ll take the smaller one.
do so / do it / do that
Replace a whole verb phrase. do so is the formal choice.
Of two things already named: the former is the first, the latter the second.
Points back to a kind of thing: such occurrences are coincidence.
eg: The landings were faked. This began with the flag.
this = the whole belief.
The far side is permanently dark. That is simply wrong.
that = the claim, dismissively.
The moon affects the tides, but it does so by a tiny amount.
do so = affect the tides.
I have two versions. I’ll send you the shorter one.
one replaces version.
They are the smaller ones.
ones, plural.
Tsunamis and supermoons sometimes coincide. Such occurrences prove nothing.
such = of that kind.
We looked at Mars and at Earth. The former has almost no atmosphere.
the former = Mars.
Coffee or tea? I would prefer the latter.
the latter = tea.
She asked me to check it, and I did so immediately.
do so replaces the whole action.
If it did so, there would be no seasons.
do so pointing back to turn on a straighter axis.
acts.careful: “That is simply wrong” and “It is simply wrong” are not equally safe. that points cleanly at an entire idea; it sends the reader looking for a noun first, and only settles on the idea if no noun fits. When you mean the whole of what was just said, write that.

write.q: Write about 180 words explaining a belief that is common where you live and either testing it or defending it. Use at least five reference words from this lesson — this, that, it, one, do so, such, the former, the latter — and make sure a reader could say exactly what each of them points back to.
write.ph: A great many people here believe…
write.model:
A great many people here believe that going outside with wet hair will make you ill. This is not a fringe view; it is what most of my family would tell you, and they would do so without hesitating.

The belief probably comes from two things happening together. Colds are commonest in winter, and winter is when going out with wet hair is most memorable. Such coincidences are exactly how these ideas survive.

The evidence is unhelpful to both sides. Being cold does not cause a viral infection; that much is settled. But some studies suggest cold air reduces the immune response in the nose, and if it does so even slightly, the folk version is not entirely wrong.

So there are two claims here — that cold causes illness, and that it makes illness likelier. The former is false. The latter may be partly true, and I have stopped arguing about it at family dinners.
